newsitem.title: UK: N. Ireland police chief sees new IRA ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: N. Ireland police chief sees new IRA ceasefire.

text.p: The Irish Republican Army will declare another ceasefire because the republican leadership still sees the advantages of peace, Northern Ireland's chief police officer said.

In an interview published in Monday's edition of The Times, Sir Hugh Annesley gave a warning that IRA guerrillas would try to stage more bomb attacks in mainland Britain and Northern Ireland before laying down their arms again.
The IRA broke a 17-month truce in February with a series of bombs in mainland Britain.
A soldier died in the first IRA bomb attack in Northern Ireland in more than two years when the guerrillas attacked the British army's headquarters near Belfast earlier this month.
Annesley, who retires as head of Northern Ireland's Royal Ulster Constabulary next month, said that "sooner or later" the IRA would abandon its campaign of violence.
"I would certainly see it as coming potentially in the next year. I have no doubt that the republican movement is deeply put out by the strong stance of the British and Irish governments," he said.
London and Dublin have excluded Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, from multi-party peace talks on Northern Ireland, saying the IRA must first end its war against British rule in the province.
Annesley said the IRA would wants to declare a new truce from a position of strength.
"I think we are in a situation where further attacks on the British mainland are probable and I think an attack within the province has moved from possible to probable," he said.
Annesley based his prediction on intelligence reports and his own judgment of the thinking of the republican leadership.

He felt Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams and chief strategist Martin McGuinness believed that long-term solutions to the problems of Northern Ireland, beset by a quarter century of sectarian and political violence, would be solved by politics and not by military force.
"I think still that Adams and McGuinness still see the advantages of peace," Annesley said.
He said one sign of a move towards a ceasefire was the IRA's plan to hold a "General Army Convention", which is the only body within the IRA that can declare a permanent end to violence.
Annesely expressed approval of the fact that fiercely pro-British "loyalist" guerrillas had maintained the ceasefire they declared two years ago, despite the latest wave of IRA violence.

But he added: "If they were pushed back into violence, and they have been very severely pushed up to now, then one would have to imagine immediate attacks on the Republic of Ireland and throughout Northern Ireland."
